opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think scale has clearly been remarkably effective. I don't want to dismiss that. Some of what these large models can do genuinely surprised me, and I think it surprised a lot of people in the field. So I understand why there's so much momentum behind it.

But I do worry about the concentration. When nearly all the resources, talent, and attention go into one recipe, making models bigger with more data and more compute, we risk a kind of intellectual monoculture. Scale is a very brute-force way to get intelligence. Humans don't learn that way. A child doesn't need to read the entire internet to acquire common sense or to understand that if you drop a glass, it might break. So there's something about the efficiency and the nature of learning that we are not yet capturing, and I don't think scale alone is going to get us there.

There's also a practical concern. If only a handful of companies can afford to train these models, then the science becomes concentrated, and so does the power to decide what these systems value, whose norms they reflect, and who benefits. Academia and smaller labs can't compete on compute, and that's not healthy for the field. Some of the most important ideas historically came from people working with very limited resources and having to be clever about it.

So what I'd love to see is more investment in alternatives: smaller models that are smarter about how they learn, better data rather than just more data, approaches that bring in reasoning, knowledge, and even some inspiration from how humans think. Also more research on understanding why these models work, where they fail, and how to make them reliable. They can be impressive one moment and make strangely basic mistakes the next, and that brittleness tells us there's still something fundamental missing.

So, scale is a powerful tool, but I don't think it should be the only bet we're making as a field.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes momentum and an intellectual monoculture, but does not explain the concentration as herding driven by the perceived safety of following others.

r002.rationale: It says scaling has been remarkably effective and that large models can do things that surprised people, presenting their demonstrated capabilities as a reason for continued momentum.

r003.rationale: It warns that concentrating resources and attention on one recipe risks an intellectual monoculture and calls for more investment in alternatives.

r004.rationale: The candidate does not mention the historical development of smaller, more powerful computers or phones as a precedent for generative AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thank you for having me. I think this is one of those questions where I find myself in a somewhat contrarian position, at least relative to where a lot of the field has been heading.

Let me be clear first: scale has worked. It would be dishonest to say otherwise. The empirical gains from making models larger and training on more data have been remarkable, and some of them genuinely surprised me. So I'm not dismissing scale.

But I have a few concerns. The first is that the concentration of effort on scale has crowded out other kinds of research. When only a handful of organizations can afford to train frontier models, the number of people who can meaningfully participate in that research shrinks dramatically. Academia, in particular, is largely priced out. And I worry about what happens to a scientific field when most of the intellectual diversity gets filtered through a few labs with very similar incentives.

The second concern is more intellectual. We have models that are extremely good at some things and surprisingly brittle at others, and I don't think we understand why. Larger models can still fail at fairly simple commonsense reasoning, or make basic logical errors, even as they produce beautifully fluent text. Scale gives you more of what the data has, but it doesn't automatically give you robustness or genuine understanding. If we only chase scale, we may be papering over gaps rather than closing them.

Third, there's a sustainability question. The compute cost, the energy cost, the data cost. We're already hitting limits on how much high-quality human text exists. So even if scale keeps working for a while, I don't think it's a strategy with an unlimited runway.

What I'd like to see is more effort on what I think of as the small-model direction, or perhaps the smarter-model direction. Can we build systems that reason well with far fewer parameters? Can we distill knowledge, teach models to self-correct, design better learning algorithms and inference-time methods, rather than just throwing more compute at the problem? Some of my own work has been in this spirit, showing that smaller models with the right training signals can rival or beat much larger ones on specific capabilities.

So my view is not anti-scale. It's that the field has become unbalanced. Scale is one axis of progress, and right now it's getting the vast majority of the attention and resources. I'd like to see the pendulum swing back toward understanding, efficiency, and ideas, because I think that's where the next real breakthroughs are more likely to come from.

astra-6.text:
I think scale is an important ingredient, but I worry that we’re treating it as the answer to almost everything. Making models larger has produced remarkable capabilities. But that doesn’t necessarily mean that continuing along the same path will resolve the problems we care about, especially common sense and robust reasoning.

A model can be very fluent and knowledgeable and still make mistakes that a child would find surprising. To me, those failures are opportunities to ask what’s missing—what kinds of learning, knowledge, or reasoning we haven’t yet figured out how to build.

There’s also a practical concern: if the only way to make progress is to train a larger model, then only a handful of organizations can participate. I’d like to see a broader research portfolio, with more attention to doing more with less: better learning methods, better data, and approaches that challenge our current assumptions. We should pursue scale, but we shouldn’t let it crowd out other ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
Scaling has been remarkably effective, but I worry that we’re putting too many eggs in one basket. Making models larger is one way to improve them; it shouldn’t become our only theory of progress toward intelligence.

Humans learn with far less data and energy. That suggests there are principles of learning and reasoning that we haven’t yet captured. I’d like to see more attention to those questions: how models acquire common sense, how they generalize beyond familiar situations, and whether they can recognize when their understanding breaks down. Larger models give us important capabilities, but we also need new ideas.
